title: Backpressure
description: Learn about backpressure mechanisms for handling load in streaming systems. Understand how to prevent system overload by controlling data flow.

data.text: Backpressure is a mechanism for handling load when a fast producer sends data to a slow consumer. Instead of letting the consumer get overwhelmed, backpressure signals the producer to slow down or buffer data.
When producers are faster than consumers, problems arise without backpressure.

items: Unbounded memory growth—consumer queues fill indefinitely
System crashes—out of memory errors
Increased latency—data sits in queues
Data loss—queues overflow
Cascading failures—overload spreads upstream

data.title: Unbounded Queues
data.text: Unbounded queues are a common source of production failures. Always bound your queues and implement backpressure.

items.title: Push Backpressure
items.description: Producer pushes data, consumer signals when it's ready. Good for pull-based systems, but requires coordination.

items.title: Pull Backpressure
items.description: Consumer pulls data when ready. Producer waits for requests. Simpler, naturally handles backpressure.

items.title: Buffering
items.description: Temporary storage between producer and consumer. Bounded queues prevent overflow. Must handle full queues.

items.title: Dropping
items.description: Drop data when consumer can't keep up. Accept data loss for system stability. Good for non-critical data.

data.text: Reactive programming builds backpressure into the data flow model.

items: Streams signal demand to producers
Producers only send when requested
Automatic flow control through the stream
No explicit coordination needed
Built into reactive frameworks (Rx, Project Reactor)

data.title: Reactive Streams
data.text: Reactive Streams standard defines backpressure protocols. Use reactive frameworks for natural backpressure handling.

items: Message queues—use bounded queues and monitoring
HTTP APIs—rate limiting, backoff, circuit breakers
Streaming systems—flow control, windowing
Databases—connection pooling, query throttling
Microservices—all of the above plus service-level controls

data.text: When your bounded queue is full, you need a strategy.

items: Block the producer—simple but can cause cascading delays
Drop new messages—lose data but protect the system
Drop oldest messages—keep newer data, accept staleness
Reject with error—let producer handle the failure
Scale the consumer—add more capacity if possible
Always use bounded queues—never unbounded
Monitor queue sizes and alert on thresholds
Implement graceful degradation when overloaded
Test backpressure behavior under load
Document your backpressure strategy
Consider the cost of dropping vs blocking

data.title: Measure and Monitor
data.text: Track queue sizes, latency, and drop rates. These metrics tell you if your backpressure strategy is working.
